title: ER triage at malloc: lifetime-predicted placement into DRAM or NV
idea: Like emergency rooms triaging on arrival, a profiler tags each allocation site with predicted object lifetime and write intensity, and the allocator places long-lived read-mostly objects directly in persistent memory at birth while only short-lived write-hot objects get DRAM.
why: Avoids later migration cost; most bytes are long-lived and read-mostly, so DRAM footprint shrinks 2-3x and long-lived state is durable.

title: Morse code: Huffman exponents decoded at line rate in controller
idea: Morse gives E a single dot: entropy-code only the exponent field of BF16/FP8 tensors per 4 KB block (about 2.5-3 bits of information in 8) and decode in a 16-lane table-driven unit in the memory controller, keeping sign and mantissa raw for fixed-latency random access.
why: Lossless ~25-30% capacity reduction on all floating-point weights and activations.

title: Eliminate hash-table overhead with succinct minimal-perfect-hash cache modules
idea: A Redis module rebuilds read-mostly keyspaces into a minimal perfect hash (about 2 bits/key) plus Elias-Fano-packed values, with a small mutable delta table merged incrementally.
why: Pointer-rich hash tables cost 50-80 B/key of overhead; density improves 3-5x.

title: Sintering: press read-mostly structures into succinct form, remelt on write
idea: Sintering fuses loose powder into a dense part. A runtime detects read-mostly pointer-based structures (hash maps, tries, B-trees, adjacency lists) and 'sinters' them into succinct static encodings: Elias-Fano, rank/select bitvectors, minimal perfect hashes. Writes go to a small mutable 'green' overlay, and the structure is re-sintered when the overlay grows too large.
why: Pointer-heavy structures use 3-10x more memory than their information content; the sintered forms get within 10-30% of entropy for indexes, graphs and routing tables.

title: Client-parked compressed KV state between conversation turns
idea: After each turn, the server sends the user's device or the nearest edge PoP a compressed, encrypted latent state of ~0.5-2 MB (MLA-style low-rank KV or a distilled gist-token set). The next request uploads it back. The datacenter then holds no per-session state across gaps of minutes to days.
why: The long-timescale residency of KV moves off scarce HBM/DRAM onto idle client storage. Datacenter session memory shrinks toward only the active-decode set.

title: Eliminate stranded DIMMs: fleet profiling plus physical DIMM redistribution
idea: A 10-person service profiles fleet memory use with eBPF, finds hosts with chronically idle DIMMs, and sends technicians to move modules into memory-starved hosts during maintenance windows.
why: Fleets typically strand 20-30% of installed DRAM; reallocating it defers new purchases by a year or more.

title: Display-fab TFT-on-glass capacitor memory panels
idea: Worsen: insist all working memory comes from 12 nm EUV wafers. Flip: build 1T1C cells with oxide TFTs on Gen-10.5 display glass at micron design rules and stack panels as a slow, multi-level bulk tier behind a small DRAM cache.
why: Cost: $30-60/m2 of processed glass at about 1 um2 per cell and 2-4 bits per cell gives about $0.1-0.25/GB, 50-100x cheaper; trades access time (us), area and refresh.

title: Silicon logic is cheap: mature-node dedup die under DRAM stacks
idea: Because a 28 nm logic die costs a fraction of DRAM per mm2, the base die of a DRAM stack runs a content-addressed dedup engine: every 64 B write is hashed (CRC64, second hash on collision), unique lines are stored once with a reference count, and a translation table maps logical lines to physical lines inside the stack.
why: Line-granular exact dedup finds 1.3-2x redundancy in VM, container and inference-replica memory where page-level dedup finds little; it trades cheap logic area for scarce DRAM bits (cost/bit).

title: Texture-compression units repurposed to hold activations compressed
idea: Inverts 'GPU texture hardware is only for graphics': activations, KV blocks or embeddings are encoded into fixed-rate block-compressed texture formats (BC/ASTC-style) and read through the GPU's existing texture samplers, which decode them in hardware at full speed.
why: Fixed-rate 4-8x compression on tolerant tensors, using silicon already installed in billions of GPUs and no new chips.

title: Return-time-predicted KV hibernation for idle chat sessions
idea: Imposed limit: an idle conversation may hold zero KV bytes in DRAM. When a user goes idle, the KV cache is dropped and only token IDs are kept; a predictor that reads typing indicators, tab focus and the user's past think-times schedules a re-prefill on spare compute a few seconds before the next message is expected.
why: Idle sessions hold a large share of KV memory in chat serving; trading cheap compute for scarce DRAM can cut resident KV 3-10x, with sub-second latency cost when the prediction is right.

title: Tax credit for certified bytes-per-task software reductions
idea: IFR: saving a byte is valued like making one. Constraint: no materials at all, so make it policy: a federal credit pays firms per GB-year of DRAM demand avoided, measured against a standardized bytes-per-task benchmark suite and audited like energy-efficiency incentives.
why: Creates a market for compression, dedup and KV-efficiency software; a 10% demand cut equals a fab's output without the $15B.

title: Frequency-domain storage of activation tensors
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: store saved activations and feature maps after a blockwise DCT/Hadamard transform with truncated high-frequency coefficients, since smooth tensors concentrate energy in few coefficients; the inverse transform is fused into the consuming kernel.
why: Training activation memory and vision/video feature caches compress 3-6x, cutting HBM capacity per accelerator.

title: DIMM reincarnation: retired DDR4 behind 28 nm CXL bridges
idea: Inverts 'retired DIMMs are e-waste': hyperscalers pull DDR4 from decommissioned servers, retest it and mount it on CXL Type-3 cards whose controller is made on existing 28 nm logic lines. The result is a slow but large tier for cold pages and KV spill.
why: Millions of DDR4 DIMMs retire each year; reusing them adds 10-25% fleet capacity at near-zero cost per bit with no new DRAM wafers.

title: Aluminum remelt: retired DDR4 recast as a CXL far tier
idea: Aluminum is infinitely recyclable; likewise decommissioned servers' DDR4 DIMMs are tested, binned and mounted on CXL Type-3 expander cards whose controller adds stronger ECC and page compression, then deployed as the cold tier under new DDR5 hosts.
why: Hyperscalers retire millions of good DIMMs a year; reuse supplies ~25-40% of a host's capacity from sunk-cost silicon, cutting new DRAM purchases and scarce-resource intensity at near-zero fab capital.

title: Retreading: remanufacture retired DIMMs into graded CXL expanders
idea: Tire retreaders reuse old carcasses. A remanufacturing line pulls DDR4/DDR5 from decommissioned servers, retests the chips, bins them by retention and speed, and remounts them on CXL expander cards whose controller maps around weak rows. The cards are sold as a warm memory tier.
why: Recovers hundreds of PB of existing DRAM from 3-5 year server refresh cycles, adding supply with no new fab capacity at an estimated 20-30% of new DRAM cost per GB.

title: Video-codec P-frames: delta-encoded memory pages against reference pages
idea: Borrowed from MPEG inter-frame coding: a CXL memory-expander controller keeps 'I-pages' as references and stores near-duplicate pages (VM clones, forked workers, fine-tuned weight variants, beam-search KV copies) as XOR/byte-delta 'P-pages' with offset hints, decoded in a ~20 ns pipeline on read. A MinHash similarity index chooses each page's reference at write-back time.
why: Capacity/cost per bit: near-duplicate (not identical) pages are invisible to exact dedup; claims 2-6x effective capacity on multi-tenant and multi-variant model hosts.

title: Hearing-aid analog: weights compute inside 3D-NAND strings
idea: From hearing aids running keyword spotters with analog in-memory compute: large-model weights live in 3D-NAND arrays operated as analog vector-matrix multipliers (string currents sum the products), so weights never occupy DRAM and only activations move.
why: 3D NAND stores roughly 10x+ more bits per wafer than DRAM, so fab water per weight bit falls ~10x and weight DRAM goes to zero.

title: Superposed tensor storage with random-sign binding keys
idea: IFR: one buffer holds many tensors at once. Closest: k low-precision tensors (e.g., gradient accumulators of k micro-batches or k LoRA deltas) are each multiplied by a random +/-1 key vector and summed into one buffer; unbinding with the same key recovers each one with noise that error-tolerant training absorbs.
why: k-fold (k~4-8) memory cut for noise-tolerant accumulators; a hyperdimensional-computing trade of noise for capacity.

title: Hourglass: retention-failed dies hold only millisecond-lived data
idea: Sand runs out on a known schedule: bin dies that fail 64 ms retention (normally scrapped or downbinned) into 'hourglass DIMMs' with refresh disabled, and let the allocator place only data with guaranteed lifetimes under 5 ms there (activations, pipeline and staging buffers) via a lifetime tag in the allocation API.
why: Recovers several percent of wafer output lost to retention fallout and removes refresh energy (fact 3) for that data; supply gain at zero fab capex.

title: Ershov hash-consing of tensor blocks across fine-tunes and agent forks
idea: Revive Ershov's 1958 hash-consing in the memory controller: every 4 KB weight or KV block is content-hashed on write and interned in a global table, so identical blocks across fine-tuned variants, unmerged adapters, forked agent contexts and replicas are stored once, and near-identical blocks are stored as base pointer plus XOR-compressed residual. Divergence triggers copy-on-write.
why: Capacity: multi-tenant pools of hundreds of partial fine-tunes and agent trees are mostly duplicate blocks; 5-50x reduction for those pools.

title: Digital-hoarder edge case: object-level access sampling exiles untouched objects
idea: From the user who opens everything and touches nothing: the memory controller samples access bits per object rather than per page via allocator-tagged address ranges, and objects untouched for a window are compacted together and exiled to compressed CXL flash with a fault-driven return path.
why: In hoarding workloads 80-95% of resident bytes are cold; object-level exile lets DRAM shrink ~10x with fab water following.

title: Repurpose installed Optane PMem as read-only weight and index tier
idea: Box: reuse × installed persistent-memory DIMMs × 256 B block × deployment × DAX-mapped read-mostly data. Fleets still holding discontinued 3D XPoint DIMMs map read-mostly data (model weights, inverted indexes, embedding tables) straight into the address space, sparing DRAM for write-heavy state.
why: Byte-addressable ~300 ns capacity already sitting in racks absorbs read-mostly working sets; no new production, so no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Datacenter spleen grades and recirculates aging memory modules
idea: The spleen filters old red blood cells and recycles their iron; a campus test station receives every pulled module, characterizes retention, hammer threshold and speed, and re-dispatches it to the tier it can still serve (hot, warm, approximate, scrap), feeding results back to procurement.
why: Supply: longer useful life for every purchased bit; 20-30% less new DRAM procured per year.

title: Magnify compression effort with neural codecs on spare tensor cores
idea: Magnify compression effort for cold pages: learned autoencoder and context-model codecs, trained per page class (heap, tensors, text), run on the accelerator's idle tensor cores to compress and decompress the cold tier instead of LZ4.
why: Spare FLOPs are cheap and bits are scarce. Cold-tier compression goes from ~2x (LZ4) to ~3-5x, so less DRAM is needed behind the hot set.

title: I/O lands in SRAM, bypassing DRAM bounce buffers entirely
idea: Reverse the I/O path: NICs and SSDs DMA straight into reserved LLC or accelerator SRAM slices under credit-based flow control, and consumers process the data there, so read-once network and storage payloads never stage in DRAM buffers or the page cache.
why: Frees the DRAM held for I/O buffers and staging (10-30% of storage and network appliance memory) and skips the DRAM round trip's 10-20 pJ/bit (fact 5).

title: Stack-distance profiler sizing each VM's DRAM to its miss-curve knee
idea: The minimum DRAM a workload needs is set by its reuse-distance distribution, not its allocation. A hardware Mattson stack-distance sampler in the memory controller (hashed address sampling with a small SHARDS-style tree) builds each VM's miss-ratio curve in real time; the hypervisor grants local DRAM up to the knee and backs the tail with compressed or CXL memory.
why: Servers carry 25-40% more DRAM than the measured knee; sizing to it cuts purchases ~20-30% at <2% slowdown.

title: One-dollar MCU lesson: SRAM-only microservers for tiny serverless functions
idea: From $1 IoT chips that have no DRAM at all: serverless functions whose working set WebAssembly static analysis proves to be under 4-8 MB run on many-core chips with only on-die SRAM and code streamed from flash; only the minority of large functions land on DRAM servers.
why: Most functions are allocated 128 MB+ but touch a few MB; running them DRAM-free cuts DRAM bits per invocation >10x, and the fab water with it.

title: Pupation: cold pointer structures metamorphose into succinct NV forms
idea: Like a caterpillar reorganizing into a compact pupa, cold pointer-rich structures (tries, graphs, inverted indexes) are rebuilt into succinct rank/select encodings (Elias-Fano, wavelet trees) stored in byte-addressable NV and queried in place without decompression.
why: Succinct forms approach entropy and are 5-20x smaller than pointer forms; data stays durable and off DRAM.

title: Internal GB-second futures market in the cluster scheduler
idea: Worsen: give every job free, fixed memory reservations sized for peak. Flip: jobs bid for memory in GB-second futures with a surge price at saturation; under-used reservations are resold as spot memory with a 1-second reclaim contract backed by compressed swap.
why: Capacity and capital: turns the 20-30% of datacenter DRAM that is stranded into sellable capacity, so 1.25-1.4x more work per installed GB.

title: Homeric bard's formulas: fleet-trained compression dictionaries in memory controllers
idea: Oral poets held whole epics in memory as reusable formulas ('rosy-fingered dawn'). A hyperscaler mines fleet memory for recurring 16-64 B fragments (object headers, vtable pointers, UTF-8 strings, protobuf tags) and trains a shared dictionary per workload class. Memory-controller compressors load it and replace the fragments with short codes.
why: On small 64 B lines, shared dictionaries beat per-line compressors by about 1.5-2x. That is +30-60% effective DRAM capacity fleet-wide.

title: Die-cast slabs: address bits imply object type, headers vanish
idea: Parts from one die-casting mold are identical, so they need no label. The runtime allocates every object of a class (a 'mold') in a 2 MB cast slab whose address bits encode the mold ID. That removes per-object headers, vtable pointers and type tags, and 64-bit references become 32-bit slab-relative offsets decoded by a hardware base register.
why: Managed heaps (Java, Python, JS, Go) spend 20-40% of memory on headers and fat pointers, so removing them gives about 1.3-1.6x effective capacity for the biggest DRAM users in cloud fleets.

title: Precision that ages: KV entries fade from FP16 to 2-bit
idea: Inverts 'a value keeps its precision for life': a background kernel demotes KV entries as they age or lose attention mass (FP16 to FP8 to INT4 to INT2), like a JPEG whose quality fades with distance, while recent and high-attention tokens stay sharp.
why: Average KV storage near 3 bits per element instead of 16: a 4-5x KV footprint cut at long context with small accuracy loss.

title: Holographer's superposition: bind thousands of key-value pairs into shared vectors
idea: A hologram spreads the whole scene across every fragment. Distant-past key-value pairs are bound by circular convolution (holographic reduced representations) and summed into a fixed bank of 64 superposition vectors per head. A query unbinds them by correlation to retrieve an approximate value, while recent tokens stay exact.
why: Memory for the distant past becomes O(1) per head instead of O(n), aimed at 10M-token agent memories. Retrieval noise grows with load.

title: Fiber speckle random projections shrink recommendation embedding tables
idea: Replace TB-scale embedding tables with compact codes. A thermally stabilized multimode fiber's speckle acts as a fixed, enormous random matrix, so a short per-ID code expands optically into a full embedding (the hashing trick at light speed). Only the codes and a small learned correction table stay in DRAM.
why: Embedding tables are the largest DRAM consumer in recommender clusters. Compresses them 10-50x.

title: Flash serves reads, DRAM only absorbs writes in inference
idea: Reverse the tier order for read-only data: model weights stream on a fixed layer schedule (so they can be prefetched perfectly) from a many-channel high-bandwidth NAND stack straight into accelerator SRAM, and DRAM/HBM is kept only for the mutable KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are often 50-80% of inference HBM; taking them out of DRAM cuts DRAM bits per served model 2-4x and sidesteps the HBM TSV tax (fact 6).

title: Transparent huge pages, fixed: per-4KB valid bitmap stops bloat
idea: Databases disable THP because 2 MB pages physically back untouched memory and bloat RSS. Give each 2 MB TLB entry a 512-bit valid bitmap read by the page-table walker so only touched 4 KB frames are physically backed, keeping TLB reach without the bloat.
why: Recovers the 10-30% of DRAM lost to huge-page bloat on memory-heavy services.

title: Grafted controller mezzanine upgrades compression without scrapping DRAM
idea: Gardeners graft new scions onto old rootstock; CXL memory modules put the DRAM on a long-lived rootstock board and the controller and compression ASIC on a pluggable mezzanine, so better compression or a new link standard is adopted by swapping a small card rather than the DRAM.
why: Capital and supply: each DRAM bit's effective capacity rises over its life (1.5x to 3x) and it outlives link generations.

title: Reject-bin DRAM becomes the approximate-data memory tier
idea: Reverse the quality order: dies and DIMMs that fail retention or weak-cell binning (already made, normally scrapped) are packaged into an 'approximate' CXL tier with masked-error semantics, holding error-tolerant data such as video frames, NN activations and low-attention KV.
why: Adds usable bits from yield loss with zero new wafer starts, so no neon excimer litho or helium-cooled etch is used; recovering 3-5% of industry yield loss adds supply on the order of a mid-size fab line.

title: Air traffic controller assigns landing slots by predicted output length
idea: Controllers schedule landings so the runway is never overbooked. A small classifier predicts each request's output length from the prompt. The scheduler reserves KV pages for the predicted trajectory and packs requests to ~95% peak occupancy instead of sizing for the worst case, preempting by swap only on mispredictions. Software only.
why: Conservative KV reservation wastes 30-60% of HBM. Predicted landing slots raise concurrency per GB 1.5-2x.

title: Provision DRAM at median compression ratio with emergency spill tier
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: size each server's physical DRAM for the median, not worst-case, compression ratio and pre-install a cushion (a small battery-backed NAND-on-CXL tier plus a pinned 3% reserve) that absorbs a ratio collapse instantly while the scheduler migrates the offending workload away.
why: Operators provision for worst case and throw away the compression win; cushioning lets 30-50% less DRAM be bought for the same virtual capacity.

title: Camel's hump storage: model-codec page compression for text heaps
idea: From camels that carry dense reserves and metabolize them on demand: cold pages of text-heavy heaps (JSON, logs, documents, prompts) are compressed by a small learned language model plus arithmetic coder on the memory controller (~10x versus ~3x for LZ) and expanded into a staging area only on touch.
why: Cuts resident DRAM for text-heavy services ~10x; fewer manufactured bits means proportionally less fab ultrapure water.

title: Row-hammer activation counters double as page-hotness telemetry
idea: Combine DDR5 per-row activation counting (PRAC, built for row-hammer defense) with OS memory tiering: expose a decayed counter summary through a mode-register/sideband read so the kernel knows exactly which rows are cold without page-table access-bit scanning, and demotes them to CXL, compressed or flash tiers.
why: Accurate, free hotness data lets 30-50% of resident pages move to cheaper tiers with little slowdown, cutting top-tier DRAM per server by about a third; reuses silicon already paid for (fact 9).

title: Hash-consing allocator merges identical immutable objects at birth
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: the language runtime interns every immutable object (strings, tuples, small records, JSON subtrees) through a hash table at allocation, so identical values become one physical object, as 1990s Lisp and ML systems did; it runs on any CPU.
why: Duplicate objects are 10-40% of heaps in data-processing services, and object-level dedup is far finer than page dedup.

title: Thousand-thread barrel cores make NAND the main memory
idea: Worsen: put all data on slow media and make the core stall on every access. Flip: build barrel processors with 1,000+ hardware threads per core (Tera MTA style) that switch every cycle, so 20-50 us SLC/TLC NAND reads are hidden and flash becomes byte-addressable main memory behind a small DRAM line buffer.
why: Cost: NAND at $0.05-0.15/GB vs DRAM at about $10+/GB, so 70-200x cheaper per GB; trades single-thread latency for throughput on graph, database and analytics work.

title: Idle tensor cores regenerate old-context KV from token IDs
idea: This adds zero masks. Decode is memory-bound, with tensor cores ~70% idle. For context older than a horizon, the server keeps only 4-byte token IDs plus a mid-layer checkpoint every N layers, and recomputes K/V in the idle compute slots of each decode step. Nanosecond-scale compute replaces seconds-scale storage.
why: Old-context KV bytes drop 50-500x for long contexts, paid for by compute that was otherwise idle.

title: Fixed-rate ZFP codec in the L2 fill path for simulation arrays
idea: Box: lossy random-access compression × L2 fill/evict path × 4×4×4 float block × fixed 8–16 bits per value × HPC fields. Arrays live in DRAM as fixed-rate ZFP blocks; a cache-side codec decompresses on fill and recompresses on eviction, so code sees plain doubles.
why: HPC mesh size per node is DRAM-bound; 4–8× capacity at error below discretization error.

title: 180 nm TCAM dedup engine for constant-time page fingerprint lookup
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: borrow the 1990s router TCAM; a 180 nm ternary CAM holds partial fingerprints of pages, each newly written or newly cold page is looked up in one cycle, and only hits are byte-verified, making dedup a continuous hardware service instead of a CPU scan.
why: KSM-style scanning costs CPU and finds duplicates late; continuous dedup recovers 10-30% of memory in VM/container hosts.

title: Printed ferroelectric-polymer cold-page tier on flex
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): P(VDF-TrFE) ferroelectric capacitors over printed oxide TFTs form a non-volatile, byte-addressable flex tier with microsecond access behind a CXL controller. The OS demotes pages untouched for two minutes or more to this tier, so DRAM holds only the working set.
why: 25-50% of datacenter DRAM is cold at any moment; a printed tier needing no EUV and no fab could shrink installed DRAM 1.3-2x, provided multi-layer printing reaches ~$1-3/GB.

title: Bistable e-paper display as its own framebuffer
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): electrophoretic and cholesteric display films are made roll-to-roll and hold an image at zero power, so signage, shelf labels, dashboards and e-readers push partial updates straight from the compositor to the pixels and drop the DRAM framebuffer entirely.
why: Billions of low-end displays carry a DRAM/SRAM framebuffer; the bistable film stores the picture itself, removing that memory and its refresh energy.

title: Goto parametron phase memory as attractor-based retrieval store
idea: Revive the 1954 parametron, which stored bits as 0 or pi oscillation phase: a university-fab array of MEMS or LC parametric oscillators, coupled through programmable capacitors that encode stored patterns, relaxes from an injected query to the nearest stored pattern. This gives associative recall of documents or KV clusters without scanning memory.
why: Vector databases and long-term memory stores sitting in DRAM become a physical attractor network, and one settling event replaces reading GBs of embeddings.

title: VMware page sharing, fixed: timing-equalized dedup with uniform write faults
idea: Transparent Page Sharing was disabled by default after Flush+Reload and Dedup-Est-Machina exploited copy-on-write timing. Re-enable cross-VM dedup but force every write to any merge-candidate page through an identical pre-allocated fault path (shared or not) and flush shared lines on cross-domain access, so the timing oracle disappears.
why: Restores the 20-40% DRAM savings TPS gave dense VDI/cloud hosts, cutting DRAM per VM at ~1-2% write-path overhead.

title: Optane Memory Mode, fixed: associative tag-in-ECC cache over CXL flash
idea: Optane's Memory Mode died on direct-mapped DRAM-cache conflict misses that exposed 300+ ns media. Replace it with a 4-way set-associative near-memory DRAM cache whose tags and way-predictor live in DDR5 ECC spare bits, fronting a cheap CXL SLC-NAND tier, with promotion only on second touch to stop cache pollution.
why: Cost per bit / DRAM scarcity: servers ship ~1/4 the DRAM for big, skewed footprints; conflict misses fall ~3-5x vs direct-mapped, keeping slowdown <10% while 75% of capacity is ~5x cheaper NAND.

title: Stochastic-resonance multi-reads recover bits from undersized gain cells
idea: For error-tolerant data (images, embeddings, low-order weight bits), shrink storage nodes to ~1 fF in a gain-cell array with non-destructive reads. Add calibrated noise to the sense reference and average 4-8 fast reads; the dither lifts the sub-threshold signal across the decision line (stochastic resonance), giving acceptable bit-error rates.
why: Creates a 'lossy tier' needing 4x less stored charge, which sidesteps the capacitor wall (fact 1). Gives 2-3x density on the ~40% of data that tolerates errors.

title: Linguist's Zipf law: precision proportional to word frequency
idea: Linguists know a few words carry most usage. Embedding and output-projection rows are sorted by token or ID frequency and quantized on a log-frequency schedule: 8-bit for the top 1%, 4-bit for the next 10%, and 2-bit codebooks for the long tail, with a learned scale per tier.
why: Rare rows contribute little loss, so vocabulary and embedding tables shrink 3-5x with negligible quality impact. This matters for 256k-vocabulary LLMs and recsys.

title: Split objects: hot fields stay, cold fields shrink and move out
idea: Po: every object is cut in half. A profile-guided compiler peels each struct into a hot part (fields touched on fast paths) and a cold part that is batch-compressed in a separate region and reached through a 4-byte handle only when rare paths need it.
why: Cold fields are often 50-70% of object bytes; peeling and compressing them cuts resident footprint 25-40% on domestic hardware.

title: DRAM-free inference pipeline across hundreds of mature-node SRAM chips
idea: IFR: no DRAM at all. Closest using only Si, Al, Cu, Ti, N and O: partition a model layer by layer across many 40-65 nm SRAM-heavy chips (TiSi2 contacts, Ti-barrier Cu, SiON/poly gates, no high-k metal gate) so every weight sits in SRAM beside its MAC, and pipeline large batches through the chain.
why: Eliminates weight DRAM entirely using idle mature-node U.S. capacity; higher cost per bit but no EUV and no scarce elements.

title: Melting snowman: MoS2 back-end scratchpad for transient activations
idea: A snowman only needs to last the afternoon: transfer monolayer MoS2 transistors (<=300 C) into the accelerator's back-end as 2T gain-cell scratchpads whose ultra-low leakage holds charge 1-10 s without refresh, sized for inter-layer activations that live only milliseconds.
why: Activations stop round-tripping through HBM; activation DRAM drops 2-5x and refresh disappears for that data.

title: Shingled zones for heaps: tenured objects append to zoned NV
idea: Like shingled-magnetic-recording drives writing bands sequentially, a generational garbage collector keeps the nursery in DRAM and promotes survivors by appending them to zoned persistent flash; reclaiming a zone copies live objects forward, matching NAND erase-block physics.
why: The tenured generation is most of a managed heap and rarely written; moves 60-80% of heap bytes from DRAM onto durable media.

title: Vector-database index fused with the attention KV cache
idea: Combine an approximate-nearest-neighbor index (IVF/HNSW over key vectors) with the KV cache: only centroids and the graph stay in DRAM, full K/V live in flash or a CXL tier, and each decode step retrieves just the top-k tokens with the highest query-key scores.
why: 10-20x less DRAM for million-token contexts, because attention mass concentrates on few tokens.

title: Nearest-neighbor KV residuals: store only how this prompt differs
idea: Po: every conversation is a rerun of another one. Incoming context is matched by embedding search to the closest cached context; its KV is stored as a low-bit quantized residual against that reference KV, extending prefix caching to near-duplicate, non-prefix content (templated documents, RAG chunks, code files).
why: Near-duplicate context is common in enterprise RAG/code workloads; residual coding could cut KV memory 3-8x beyond exact prefix sharing.

title: Compiler-inferred regions shrink garbage-collector headroom to 1.1x
idea: Imposed limit: a managed heap gets 10% headroom instead of 100-200%. Escape analysis assigns allocations to lexical regions that are freed in bulk, and hardware-assisted read barriers allow concurrent compaction with no semispace copy reserve.
why: JVM, Go and .NET services often provision 2-3x their live data for GC; cutting the headroom recovers 30-50% of their DRAM.

title: Swap discarded bad-row DIMMs for map-carrying discount DIMMs
idea: Substitute 'reject' with 'map and avoid'. Modules with failed rows or banks beyond post-package-repair capacity ship with a bad-address map in the SPD vendor area; firmware hands it to the OS, which never allocates those pages (as badram/memmap already allow). JEDEC signaling is untouched.
why: Raises module yield by a few percent at a discount price tier, adding usable supply through today's interface.

title: Artificial-reef carriers house retired DDR4 DIMMs as CXL memory
idea: Coral reefs grow on sunken wrecks; a CXL Type-3 carrier card with standard DIMM slots and an inline compression engine lets operators move retired DDR4 RDIMMs into new servers as a compressed second tier, with tool-less DIMM swaps and the carrier itself reused across server generations.
why: Supply: returns decommissioned DDR4 to service; 30-50% less new DDR5 per server.

title: Holographic superposition stores many pairs per vector
idea: Worsen: give each key-value pair its own exclusive memory slot. Flip: bind keys to values in 10k-dimensional hypervectors and superpose hundreds of pairs into one vector, retrieving by unbinding plus a clean-up codebook, for associative caches and semantic memory.
why: Cost: 100x+ more pairs per stored bit for approximate associative recall; trades exactness and capacity-dependent noise.

title: Freeze-drying: lyophilize idle tenants, rehydrate in milliseconds
idea: Freeze-drying removes water but keeps structure. An idle container, VM or LLM session is 'freeze-dried' by dropping all regenerable state (page cache, JIT code, allocator slack, KV that can be recomputed from tokens) and compressing the dry residue into a flash tier. An access-order trace is recorded so that rehydration prefetches data in the exact order the process will need it.
why: Clouds keep 30-60% of DRAM on idle or warm tenants; freeze-drying shrinks warm residency 5-20x while keeping wake time around 10-50 ms.

title: Memory-efficiency label: GB-hours per transaction disclosure standard
idea: This adds zero masks. A federal cloud procurement rule, plus an Energy-Star-like label, requires software vendors and cloud services to report resident GB-hours per standard transaction or per inference token, with bid credits for each halving.
why: A years-scale incentive shift toward lean software, with 10-30% memory demand reduction across public procurement during the shortage.

title: Organic-TFT event backplane makes the sensor emit only changes
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a printed organic photodiode array with a printed organic-TFT comparator in each pixel holds the last value on a pixel capacitor and fires only when intensity moves past a threshold. The result is a cheap, large-area event camera whose output stream needs no full-frame buffer.
why: Static scenes dominate surveillance and industrial vision; change-only output shrinks buffering DRAM 10-50x for those workloads.

title: Lineage paging: drop recomputable pages, rebuild them on fault
idea: Inverts 'data must be stored to be kept': the kernel records a lineage (source file + offset + transform such as decompress, JIT, parse or decode) for derived pages. Under pressure it evicts them without writing them anywhere, and on a fault it rebuilds them by replaying the transform on a spare core, like Spark lineage applied to the page cache and runtime heaps.
why: Derived data (decompressed caches, JIT code, parsed configs, decoded media) is often 15-30% of resident memory; reclaiming it with no swap I/O cuts DRAM need by that share.

title: Zone refining: sweep high-entropy lines to one end of memory
idea: Zone refining drives impurities to one end of a silicon ingot. Likewise a background sweeper scans memory, measures the entropy of each line, and moves incompressible lines (encrypted, already compressed, random) into a dedicated 'impurity' region. The remaining pages become pure, zero-rich and low-entropy, so a cheap fixed-function line compressor gets 2-4x on them without a heavyweight per-page algorithm.
why: Page compression averages only about 1.5x mainly because a few random lines spoil each page; segregating them raises the gain on memory-expansion tiers toward 2-3x.

title: Sodium spikes: streaming transformers store only the KV that fires
idea: Like a neuron's Na+ action potential that fires only past threshold, a video/audio streaming model compares each new frame's token KV with the co-located token of the previous frame and stores a new entry only if the change exceeds a learned per-layer threshold; unchanged tokens become 2-byte back-references.
why: Static-camera, screen and speech streams repeat 70-95% of tokens frame to frame; KV for long streaming contexts shrinks 5-20x (density, cost/bit).

title: Thirty-year PLC discipline: static region memory for cloud services
idea: From industrial PLCs that run for decades with no heap: compile services with region inference and per-request arenas so peak memory is proven at build time, eliminating allocator fragmentation and garbage-collector headroom; the scheduler bin-packs services by proven peak instead of observed max plus margin.
why: Managed runtimes reserve 1.5-3x live heap for GC and fragmentation; static regions can cut server DRAM provisioning 30-60%.

title: Strowger bank switching with university MEMS relays for memory pooling
idea: Revive 8-bit bank switching and Strowger stepping switches: an array of university-fabricated ohmic MEMS relays physically re-points DDR channels between hosts, so a memory module moves to another server in microseconds with no copy, no CXL controller and no protocol latency once connected.
why: Racks provision memory for average rather than peak demand through passive re-pointing, ~30% less DRAM, without the cost and latency of CXL switches.

title: Restaurant cook-to-order: store token IDs, recompute KV on demand
idea: Borrowed from kitchens that cook to order instead of holding a buffet: long contexts are kept as token IDs (2 bytes/token) and the KV for any needed span is re-prefilled in compute-dense bursts into SRAM tiles just before attention, with only a small recent window kept resident.
why: At rest, per-token state drops from ~100 KB-1 MB of KV to 2 bytes; no long-lived volatile state means nothing to refresh, trading spare FLOPs for capacity.

title: Scrap remelt: near-capacity code, refetch master copy on decode failure
idea: Foundries simply remelt bad castings. Clean data that can be fetched again (page cache, model weights, container images) sits in 1%-BER cells under a near-capacity 4 KB LDPC code with only about 10-12% overhead and a deliberately high failure rate of about 1e-6 per page read. When decoding fails, the page is refetched from SSD or a remote master, which is cheap because it is rare.
why: Accepting rare decode failures instead of guaranteeing 1e-15 roughly halves the ECC margin, and lets the largest DRAM consumer, caches of durable data, live in cheap flaky cells.

title: Fan-deck ordering: codebook indices where one flip yields a similar shade
idea: Paint fan decks put similar shades on adjacent cards, so grabbing the wrong one still looks right. For vector-quantized weights and embeddings, codebook indices are assigned by simulated annealing so that codewords whose indices differ by one bit are nearest neighbors in vector space (a Gray-like assignment). Indices are stored raw in 1%-BER cells, and a flip swaps in a nearly identical codeword.
why: Makes 2-3 bit/weight VQ (5-8x smaller than FP16) tolerant of 1% raw BER with no ECC; the assignment cuts flip distortion about 5-10x versus random index order.

title: Semantic snapshots: background apps keep only re-creatable state
idea: Imposed limit: a background phone app gets 2 MB. The OS makes each app serialize a semantic snapshot (navigation stack, form inputs, scroll positions, auth tokens) and then discards its heap; on relaunch the app rehydrates from the snapshot and a cached UI layout instead of restoring the whole heap.
why: Phones ship 12-16 GB mainly to keep apps warm; semantic snapshots could keep the same perceived warmth at 6-8 GB, and phones take roughly a third of all DRAM bits.

title: Expiring allocations: memory pages with a built-in death date
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. Every allocation carries a TTL set by the programmer or inferred by the runtime (caches, session state, speculative buffers); the OS and memory controller reclaim expired pages without any free() call and stop refreshing those rows the moment they expire.
why: Cloud heaps carry 20-40% stale cache/session data nobody frees; TTL reclamation cuts resident footprint ~20-30% and drops refresh energy on dead rows (fact 3).

title: Datacenter-wide prompt-prefix KV cache on flash servers
idea: Combine content-addressed storage with LLM prefill: KV blocks for common prefixes (system prompts, documents, tool schemas) are hashed by token sequence and stored once on NAND-heavy cache servers, and inference GPUs fetch matching prefix blocks over RDMA instead of recomputing them or pinning them in HBM.
why: Deduplicates the large share of KV repeated across users, cutting per-GPU KV footprint and prefill compute, built entirely from DUV-made NAND and mature networking.

title: Scarcity chargeback: bill teams the real price of gigabyte-hours
idea: Po: every line of code shows its memory price tag. Enterprises and agencies charge internal teams the current spot price of U.S.-made DRAM per GB-hour, and CI gates block merges that push a service past its byte budget without sign-off.
why: Makes memory cost visible where it is decided; chargeback programs typically cut consumption 15-30% within a year with no new hardware.

title: Refresh-piggybacked in-situ recompression by the memory logic die
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: DRAM must open every row each refresh window anyway; the HBM/CXL logic die issues column reads into rows already opened for refresh to scan, dedup-fingerprint and recompress cold pages, so compaction rides on maintenance activations instead of adding its own.
why: Turns refresh (16-33% of idle power) into useful work; continuous compaction at near-zero added activation energy, enabling 1.3-2x effective capacity.

title: Ice-storage KV: precompute corpus attention caches off-peak into NV
idea: Like buildings that freeze ice at night to cool by day, compute KV caches for frequently retrieved RAG documents and system prompts off-peak and store them in persistent flash; at query time they are streamed in and position-corrected rather than prefilled and held in DRAM.
why: Removes repeated prefill and replicated DRAM caches of shared documents; 3-5x DRAM saving in RAG serving.

title: Sushi conveyor: weights circulate a ring, each chip grabs its plate
idea: Model layers circulate continuously on an optical/SerDes ring of accelerators like plates on a kaiten-sushi belt; each chip computes on the layer passing it and holds only a 2-3 layer window locally instead of a full or gathered copy.
why: Per-chip weight memory drops by roughly the ring size while ring bandwidth, not HBM capacity, sets throughput; attacks the HBM capacity tax.

title: Swap all-DRAM main memory for a DRAM cache over SLC NAND
idea: Substitute most DRAM capacity with low-latency SLC NAND on a CXL device. A hardware-managed DRAM cache of about 1/8 of capacity sits in front, with page-level hot/cold tracking and a sector write-back buffer to protect endurance.
why: Most server memory is cold at any instant, so DRAM per server falls 4-8x for in-memory databases, caches and VM hosts, replaced by non-EUV NAND bits.

title: CTSS roll-out during user think time with keystroke-predicted roll-in
idea: Revive CTSS swapping between interactive turns: a chat session's KV is rolled out to CXL or flash as soon as a reply finishes, and the client streams typing telemetry (focus, keystroke cadence, draft length) so a predictor rolls the KV back into HBM in the last 1-2 s before the user hits send.
why: Users spend 20-120 s between turns versus ~5 s of generation; HBM held per concurrent session falls 5-20x without the recompute penalty of plain eviction.

title: Procurement cap on DRAM per inference, with printed-media credits
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): federal AI procurement sets a maximum number of DRAM bytes per served token or session and grants credits for verified printed or roll-to-roll media that hold frozen data (weights, shared prefixes, golden pages), creating guaranteed demand for domestic printed offload products.
why: Policy pull speeds the deployment of DRAM-sparing architectures and moves a measurable share of government AI DRAM demand onto domestic printed media.

title: Prediction-residual codec for simulation fields and time series
idea: IFR: memory stores only surprise. Closest: a memory-controller codec stores HPC fields and telemetry as entropy-coded residuals from a predictor (previous timestep, neighbour stencil), like video P-frames, decoded losslessly on access.
why: 3-10x footprint reduction for smooth physical fields in climate, CFD and sensor workloads.

title: Shared parking for memory: co-locate day and night workloads
idea: Like office parking reused by residents at night, pair anti-correlated workloads (daytime inference, night batch training/ETL) on one DRAM pool and swap working sets via fast NVMe snapshots at shift change, sizing DRAM to the peak of the sum rather than the sum of peaks.
why: Peak-of-sum vs sum-of-peaks can save 30-45% of fleet DRAM where diurnal patterns are strong.

title: Burroughs B5000 segment descriptors carrying a per-object codec
idea: Revive B5000 descriptors and presence bits: every allocation gets a hardware descriptor with exact length, presence bit and codec ID (zero, constant, delta, dictionary, bf16-exponent entropy), and touching an absent or compressed segment traps to a decompress engine in the memory controller. Segments are stored at their compressed byte size, so there is no 4 KB/2 MB page rounding.
why: Capacity: removes page-granularity fragmentation (10-30% in KV block pools and heaps) and adds 1.5-2.5x typed compression, about 2-3x effective server DRAM.

title: Follow-the-sun memory: batch work chases idle DRAM across continents
idea: Rearrange workloads in time and space: batch inference, embedding generation and analytics move every few hours to regions whose interactive demand is in its nightly trough, so each region's DRAM is sized for a flattened global load instead of its local peak.
why: Peak-to-average DRAM provisioning of ~1.6-2x shrinks toward ~1.2x, so 20-35% fewer DIMMs are bought; pure orchestration with no neon or helium.

title: Per-package 180 nm companion die doing wide-slow line compression
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: instead of one fast advanced-node compression engine, wire-bond a cheap 180 nm companion die beside each DRAM die in the package; each handles only its own chip's x8 slice with a 256-bit-wide internal datapath at 100-200 MHz running BDI/FPC compression, so segmentation makes slow old silicon fast enough.
why: Adds transparent 1.4-2x line compression to commodity modules using fully depreciated 200 mm fabs, with no advanced-node controller redesign.

title: Hoffmann kiln: compute wave rides the refresh sweep across banks
idea: In a Hoffmann ring kiln the fire travels around the stationary bricks. Refresh already opens every row on a schedule, so simple bank-level ALUs work on each row while it is open: scans, popcounts, zero-detection, dedup hashing, entropy measurement and scrubbing. Memory-saving services thus ride a 'fire zone' that marches through DRAM at no extra activation cost.
why: Background services such as dedup hashing and choosing cold pages to compress currently take host bandwidth; riding on refresh activations (about 46 fJ/bit already paid) makes them nearly free.

title: Magnify the pool to a regional spot market for stranded DRAM
idea: Magnify the memory pool from the host to the region: clouds sell stranded DRAM (on hosts whose cores are sold out) as a spot-priced remote cache/swap tier over RDMA, with preemption notice and automatic fallback to flash.
why: 25-50% of cloud DRAM sits stranded at any moment. Monetizing it raises fleet memory utilization ~1.2-1.5x, which lowers new DRAM purchases.

title: Bit-plane segmented KV cache with attention-gated plane residency
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: split every FP16 KV vector into a high plane (sign, exponent, top mantissa bits) and a low-mantissa plane stored in separate pages; only high planes stay in HBM, low planes live in CXL/LPDDR or NVMe and are fetched only for tokens whose coarse attention score (computed from high planes alone) lands in the top-k. Resolves 'keep all context' vs 'keep little memory' by holding every token coarsely and few tokens fully, losslessly.
why: KV cache dominates long-context serving memory; ~2-3x less HBM per session with a lossless fallback, so fewer HBM stacks (HBM TSV tax, cost/bit).

title: AMD HBCC, fixed: hardware-paged HBM cache with attention-aware prefetch
idea: Vega's High-Bandwidth Cache Controller paged system memory into VRAM in hardware but died because games fit in VRAM anyway. Revive it for LLM serving: HBM becomes a hardware-managed page cache over host LPDDR/CXL, and the prefetcher uses the previous decode step's attention-score sparsity to fetch only KV pages likely to be attended next.
why: HBM per GPU can drop 2-4x for long-context serving (HBM costs ~3x wafer area per bit); decode access is predictable enough to hide the far-tier latency.

title: Porous page mapping backs only written 256-byte chunks
idea: TRIZ #31 Porous materials: a 180 nm memory-side translation chip makes each 4 KB (or 2 MB huge) page 'porous'; only the 256 B chunks actually written get physical backing, tracked by a per-page 16-bit occupancy mask, and unwritten holes read as zero and cost nothing.
why: Internal fragmentation and huge-page bloat waste 10-30% of DRAM in sparse heaps and hash tables; recovered with no software changes.

title: Pointer dehydration: hardware shrinks 64-bit pointers on eviction
idea: Like dehydrating food for storage, the memory controller detects 64-bit pointers in evicted cache lines (high bits match a region-base register) and stores them as 32-bit region offsets, packing a 64 B line into 32-40 B; rehydration on fill is a single add.
why: Pointer-heavy workloads (graphs, JVM, Python, databases) are 30-50% pointers; transparent 1.3-1.6x capacity without software changes.
